To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the infant mortality rates for Mexican-origin women who give birth in the United States are significantly lower than those experienced in Mexico, and that these favorable rates are not artificially caused by the migration of Mexican-origin mothers and their infants to Mexico after the infants are born.

(1) infant mortality rates for the first week of infants’ lives among Mexican immigrants in the United States are lower than those experienced for non-Hispanic whites, and (2) infant mortality rates are not lower among Mexican immigrants because of the out-migration to Mexico of infants who die in the United States.

(1) infant mortality is lower among Mexican-origin women, both immigrant and native-born; (2) infant mortality is lowest among infants born to Mexican-origin immigrant women, and (3) the lower infant mortality experienced by infants born to Mexican immigrant mothers cannot be explained away by the out-migrating of Mexican mothers and their infants.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the infant mortality rates of the Mexican-origin population of the United States.
the epidemiologic paradox, which has been defined in the literature as the observation that certain health outcomes are better for immigrants than for their U.S.-born counterparts.
the infant mortality paradox, which is the opposite of the mortality paradox.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the Mexican-origin population of the United States, as a whole, exhibits the epidemiologic paradox.
the epidemiologic paradox is real and is not an artifact caused by the selective out-migration of the Mexican-origin population, as some recent studies seem to imply.
the Mexican immigrant mortality advantage is a true phenomenon, at least for infant mortality.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the epidemiologic paradox is real, and the selective out-migration argument is not.
the Mexican-origin population, whether immigrant or U.S. born, experiences infant mortality rates that are comparable to or even lower than those experienced in the non-Hispanic population.

The main takeaway from our work is that

the Mexican-origin population, whether born in Mexico or born in the United states, experiences lower rates of infant mortality than other groups in the U.S., and that these favorable rates cannot be explained by out-migration.
infant mortality is a good indicator of the health of a population, even among the Mexican-origin group, which has been shown to have favorable mortality rates among older age groups.
the epidemiologic paradox is not limited to the elderly Mexican-origin population in this country; rather it appears to extend to infants as well.
